notes.audience: Các lập trình viên, sysadmin và self-hoster tại Việt Nam đang quản lý từ 2 VPS/server Linux trở lên, muốn quản lý tập trung trên một giao diện web trực quan thay vì SSH từng server.
notes.angle: Khác với 1Panel thu phí bản Pro mới cho tính năng Multi-node hay Cockpit chỉ thao tác phiên SSH cục bộ, ServerOS Panel cho phép tự host miễn phí quản lý tập trung toàn bộ dàn VPS qua một agent Rust kết nối ngược an toàn, tích hợp sẵn MCP cho AI.

facts.fact: Bản miễn phí 1Panel OSS không hỗ trợ quản lý multi-node (nhiều máy chủ), tính năng này bị giới hạn riêng cho bản Pro và Enterprise trả phí.
Cockpit hoạt động bằng cách tương tác trực tiếp với phiên đăng nhập hệ điều hành Linux thật ngay trên trình duyệt thay vì hoạt động như một hệ thống quản lý ứng dụng tập trung.
facts.quote: Cockpit interacts directly with the operating system from a real Linux session in a browser.

facts.fact: ServerOS cho phép tự host (Self-hosted) panel mã nguồn mở hoàn toàn miễn phí trên VPS riêng.
facts.quote:
Self-hosted
Free

The open-source panel on your own server.

facts.fact: Panel ServerOS được viết bằng PHP 8.4, mã nguồn mở theo giấy phép AGPL-3.0.
Agent cài trên các VPS con (serverosd) là một file thực thi nhị phân tĩnh duy nhất viết bằng Rust, tự động nhận diện ứng dụng đang chạy mà không cần khởi động lại.
facts.quote: a single static binary that connects out to the panel, discovers what is already running, adopts it without a restart

facts.fact: VPS con kết nối với Panel không cần mở bất kỳ port inbound nào; agent chủ động kết nối outbound TLS 1.3 qua port 443/8443 bằng chứng chỉ cấp lúc ghi danh.
facts.quote: There is no inbound port: the daemon dials the panel over TLS 1.3 on 443 with a certificate issued at enrolment, and reconnects on its own.

facts.fact: Lần quét đầu tiên của agent trên VPS là read-only, không làm khởi động lại dịch vụ hay ghi đè bất kỳ file cấu hình nào hiện có.
facts.quote: The first scan is read-only: it finds your sites, databases, workers and containers and shows them as services. Nothing is restarted and no config is rewritten.

facts.fact: Mọi thao tác yêu cầu quyền root của agent đều được ghi nhật ký bằng ngôn ngữ rõ ràng vào file actions.log trước khi thực thi.
facts.quote: every privileged action is written to /var/log/serveros/actions.log in plain English before it happens

facts.fact: ServerOS hỗ trợ tạo mạng riêng ảo WireGuard giữa các máy chủ cho từng dự án với giao diện mạng có tên định dạng sos{network}.
facts.quote: The network job gives a project its own WireGuard network across machines. Each machine gets an interface named sos{network}

facts.fact: Agent hỗ trợ tích hợp sẵn reverse proxy gồm Caddy hoặc Nginx, và firewall gồm UFW, nftables hoặc iptables.
facts.quote:
proxy = "caddy"      # caddy | nginx | none
firewall = "ufw"     # ufw | nftables | iptables | none

facts.fact: Trên phiên bản dịch vụ đám mây (hosted), ServerOS tính phí theo số lượng máy chủ (£5/tháng cho gói Essential 1 máy, £12/tháng cho Pro 5 máy), không giới hạn số app.
facts.quote:
Essential

For individual developers.

£5/month

Start free
1 machine

facts.fact: Thư mục cài đặt mặc định của ServerOS self-hosted trên máy chủ là /opt/serveros.
Khi ngừng sử dụng ServerOS trên VPS con, chỉ cần chạy lệnh ngắt kết nối mà không ảnh hưởng hay làm gián đoạn các dịch vụ đang chạy.
facts.quote: Run serverosd disconnect on the server. Every service keeps running exactly as it is.

caveats: Bắt buộc phải có tên miền riêng và cấu hình 2 bản ghi A: một cho domain chính của panel và một cho wildcard (*.domain) vì các workspace nằm trên subdomain.

VPS cài panel phải mở các cổng 80, 443 và cổng 8443 (để agent các server con kết nối vào). Nếu chạy qua Cloudflare Tunnel thì máy con vẫn phải kết nối trực tiếp đến gateway qua port 8443 không qua proxy.
Agent serverosd bắt buộc chạy bằng quyền root trên máy chủ con (cần systemd trên amd64 hoặc arm64).
Mặc định panel tự gửi ping thống kê ẩn danh mỗi ngày về serveros.com (cần tắt thủ công bằng biến SERVEROS_TELEMETRY=false trong .env).
Agent serverosd mặc định tự gửi báo cáo lỗi về Sentry khi bị crash nếu không tắt qua cấu hình SERVEROS_ERROR_REPORTS=0.
gaps: Panel ServerOS tiêu tốn bao nhiêu tài nguyên RAM và CPU tối thiểu khi chạy toàn bộ stack Docker Compose (PHP, Redis, Gateway) ở trạng thái nghỉ?
ServerOS có kho ứng dụng cài đặt 1-click phong phú (165+ app như 1Panel) hay chủ yếu tối ưu cho việc deploy Git, container và cấu hình thủ công?
Hệ điều hành không sử dụng systemd (như Alpine Linux chạy OpenRC) có thể cài đặt làm node con được không?
Có hỗ trợ giao diện tiếng Việt trên web panel hay chỉ có tiếng Anh?

## serveroshq/panel (https://github.com/serveroshq/panel)
Description: The open source ServerOS panel: one place to run the Linux servers you already own.
Homepage: https://serveros.com
Language: PHP; license: AGPL-3.0; created 2026-11-09; last push 2026-11-12
Latest release: v1.3.2 (2026-11-12)
README (start):
ServerOS panel

One place to run the Linux servers you already own.

  
  
  
  
  

  

ServerOS runs the Linux servers you already own from one place. Connect a VPS from any provider with one command, then deploy apps, sites and databases, watch them, back them up and fix them, without living in a terminal. Your servers stay with your provider, on your account.

This repo is the panel, the web app you and your team work in. Each server runs [serverosd](https://github.com/serveroshq/daemon), a small daemon the panel talks to. [serveros.com](https://serveros.com) runs this same panel as a hosted service.

## What's in it

- **Machines**: connect a server with one command, see CPU, memory and disk, and install updates.
- **Services and projects**: deploy from Git or a template, with domains and HTTPS, and copy a project to a test environment before it goes live.
- **Backups, monitors and logs**: scheduled backups, uptime checks with alerts, status pages, and every service's logs in one place.
- **Workflows**: run steps on a schedule, on a push or by hand, like deploy, check and promote.
- **Teams**: members, roles, two-factor sign-in and an activity log.
- **AI and the API**: an MCP server and an API, so your own tools and assistants can work with your servers.

## Self-hosting

You need a Linux server with Docker, ports 80, 443 and 8443 open, and a domain like `panel.example.com` with two A records pointing at the server: one for `panel.example.com` and one for `*.panel.example.com`.

Then run this on the server:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/serveroshq/panel/main/docker/self-hosted/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- --domain=panel.example.com --email=you@example.com
```

It installs Docker if it's missing, runs the official image (`ghcr.io/serveroshq/panel`) and prints a setup code. Open `https://panel.example.com`, enter it, and the installer walks you through email and your first account. `serveros-panel setup-code` shows the code again if you lose it.

Then connect your servers from Machines › Connect machine. Each one runs [serverosd](https://github.com/serveroshq/daemon), the open source daemon, which connects out to your panel on port 8443.

[docs/self-hosting.md](docs/self-hosting.md) covers the rest: building the community edition yourself, installing without Docker, upgrades, backups, connecting machines, and the anonymous daily ping (and how to turn it off).

## Editions

| Edition                                     | What's in it                                                          | License                                    |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Community, built from this repo             | The panel                                                             | [AGPL-3.0](LICENSE), free                  |
| Official image (`ghcr.io/serveroshq/panel`) | The panel plus `serveroshq/panel-ee`, off until you add a license key | AGPL-3.0, and panel-ee under its own terms |
| [serveros.com](https://serveros.com)        | The panel, hosted for you                                             | A paid service                             |

Without a key, the official image works exactly like the community edition. A license turns on single sign-on, SCIM, custom roles, your own domains and the other paid features, with nothing to reinstall. [LICENSING.md](.github/LICENSING.md) explains what that means for you. The daemon is [AGPL-3.0](https://github.com/serveroshq/daemon/blob/main/LICENSE) too.

## Development

You need PHP 8.4, Composer, Node 22 and npm. SQLite works out of the box.

```sh
composer setup   # install, .env, key, migrate, build
composer dev     # the panel, queue worker, logs and Vite together
```

Workspaces live on subdomains, so set these in `.env` and open `http://serveros.localhost:8000`:

```dotenv
APP_URL=http://serveros.localhost:8000
APP_DOMAIN=serveros.localhost
SESSION_DOMAIN=.serveros.localhost
```

[CONTRIBUTING.md](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) has the full setup, the tests and checks CI runs, and how pull requests are reviewed. On Linux, [docker/dev](docker/dev/README.md) runs it all in Docker.

## Help and contributing

- Docs: [docs.serveros.com](https://docs.serveros.com)
- Questions and ideas: [Discussions](https://github.com/serveroshq/panel/discussions)
- Chat: [Discord](https://discord.gg/serveros)
- Bugs: [Issues](https://github.com/serveroshq/panel/issues/new/choose)

Found a security problem? Please don't open an issue; follow [SECURITY.md](.github/SECURITY.md).

Before you open a pull request, read [CONTRIBUTING.md](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md). Everyone who takes part follows the [Code of Conduct](.github/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), and first-time contributors sign the [CLA](.github/CLA.md) with a comment on their pull request.

## What is 1Panel?

1Panel is a modern, open-source Linux server management panel and a lightweight AI management platform. Through an intuitive web interface, it provides users with comprehensive, one-stop server management capabilities:
- **AI Management**: Offers a unified management platform from bare metal to agents (Metal-to-Agent). It integrates an AI gateway, and Skills Hub, while supporting centralized management of agents and models.
- **Efficient Visual Operations**: Easily manage Linux servers through a web-based GUI, streamlining tasks such as host monitoring, file management, database management, and container management.
- **Rapid Website Deployment**: Deeply integrates with popular website builders like WordPress and Halo. It enables one-click domain binding and SSL certificate configuration, significantly lowering the barrier to website creation.
- **Curated App Store**: Features a built-in store of high-quality open-source applications, providing one-click installation and upgrade services to effortlessly extend server capabilities.
- **Enterprise-Grade Security**: Deploys applications based on container technology to effectively minimize vulnerability exposure. It also provides security features such as WAF and log auditing to ensure comprehensive server protection.
- **One-Click Data Backup**: Supports one-click backup and restoration, and integrates with various cloud storage solutions to ensure data security and prevent loss.

## What is Cockpit?

Cockpit is an interactive server admin interface. It is easy to use and very lightweight.
Cockpit interacts directly with the operating system from a real Linux session in a browser.

Cockpit makes Linux discoverable, allowing sysadmins to easily perform tasks such as starting
containers, storage administration, network configuration, inspecting logs and so on.

Jumping between the terminal and the web tool is no problem. A service started via Cockpit
can be stopped via the terminal. Likewise, if an error occurs in the terminal, it can be seen
in the Cockpit journal interface.

You can also easily add other machines that have Cockpit installed and are accessible via SSH and jump
between these hosts.

## Installation

> [!NOTE]
> An installation guide can be found at [cockpit-project.org/running.html](https://cockpit-project.org/running.html). Some systems may need extra work, read about it in our [FAQ](https://cockpit-project.org/faq.html#installation)

Cockpit is [available in numerous Linux distributions](https://repology.org/project/cockpit/versions) and is usually packaged as `cockpit`. 

### Flatpak 'Cockpit Client'

We also provide a Flatpak app called [Cockpit Client](https://flathub.org/en/apps/org.cockpit_project.CockpitClient) which includes SSH login support to Linux servers.

Do I have to move my servers anywhere?

No. ServerOS runs on the servers you already have, with whichever provider you already pay. Connect one and it stays exactly where it is, on your bill.

What happens to what’s already running?

Nothing. The first scan is read-only: it finds your sites, databases, workers and containers and shows them as services. Nothing is restarted and no config is rewritten.

What does the server need?

Linux with systemd, on an amd64 or arm64 machine, plus curl and outbound HTTPS on port 443. You run the install command as root. No inbound ports need to be opened.

Is it safe to put a daemon on my server?

The daemon makes its own key on the server, which never leaves it, and holds one outbound mutual-TLS connection to the panel. It can only do a fixed list of things, asks before anything destructive, and writes every action to a log on your server. How ServerOS keeps your servers safe

What if I stop using ServerOS?

Run serverosd disconnect on the server. Every service keeps running exactly as it is. Remove the machine in the panel, and uninstall the daemon whenever you like.

What counts as a machine?

Each server with the daemon connected. Essential covers one, Pro up to five and Business up to 25. Apps and sites on them are unlimited.

ServerOS daemon

The small agent that connects your servers to ServerOS.

    

serverosd is the one thing ServerOS installs on a machine: a single static binary that connects out to the panel, discovers what is already running, adopts it without a restart, and does the deploying, backing up, and watching on the panel's behalf.

It runs as root, because installing and updating packages, editing firewall rules, and driving systemd and Docker need root. It is not a remote shell: everything it can do is a fixed, reviewed list in crates/daemon-capability, every privileged action is written to /var/log/serveros/actions.log in plain English before it happens, and the things it will never do (read /etc/shadow, read SSH private keys, leave permitted directories, phone anywhere but the panel and configured storage) are tests, not prose.

Install
curl -fsSL https://serveros.com/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- --token=ENROL_TOKEN

The script downloads the binary, verifies its checksum, and runs serverosd enrol, which prints every step. There is no inbound port: the daemon dials the panel over TLS 1.3 on 443 with a certificate issued at enrolment, and reconnects on its own.

serverosd status        what the daemon is doing
serverosd inventory     a read-only scan of what is running here
serverosd doctor        checks, each with a fix
serverosd update        check for a release, or --to X to install one
serverosd disconnect    stop management; leave every service running
serverosd uninstall     remove ServerOS and print what went and what stayed

Layout

One Cargo workspace, one crate per concern. Each crate's lib.rs says what it is for; parsers are pure functions tested against fixtures so the suite runs on any platform, and only the thin readers touch /proc, systemd, or the Docker socket.

Crate	What it owns
daemon-core	Paths, daemon.toml, build info, secret redaction, error reports
daemon-protocol	The versioned wire protocol; one driver per major
daemon-audit	actions.log
daemon-capability	The privileged operation set and the broker that gates it
daemon-http	The small HTTPS client for enrolment and release downloads
daemon-state	state.db: job ledger, telemetry ring buffer, outbox
daemon-identity	Keypair, CSR, client certificate, enrolment
daemon-transport	The outbound mTLS control channel, heartbeat, reconnect
daemon-telemetry	Machine facts, procfs samples, derived signals
daemon-inventory	Discovery: listeners, systemd, Docker, web servers, cron, TLS
daemon-import	Enrichment, honest previews, adoption, un-adoption
daemon-services	The adoption ledger and the systemd and Docker adapters
daemon-jobs	Durable, idempotent jobs with timeouts and streamed output
daemon-files	Symlink-safe file operations inside permitted roots
daemon-streams	Log tails and PTY sessions
daemon-deploy	Fetch by commit, build, health, Caddy swap, rollback
daemon-backup	Native dumps and tar, retention, pre-restore snapshots, S3
daemon-supervisor	Self-health and the resource budget
daemon-selfupdate	Signed, policy-gated updates with automatic rollback
daemon-uninstall	The manifest of what ServerOS created, and its removal
daemon-network	Project networks: WireGuard interfaces, their firewall rules, forwarders
serverosd	The binary: CLI, control loop, job handler, workers
release-tool	Key generation, signing, and manifests for CI
Building
make build          # debug build
make test           # the whole suite
make clippy         # lints, warnings denied
make linux-check    # type-check for Linux from macOS via Docker
make e2e-networks   # project networks and data copies on real WireGuard, in Docker
make release        # static musl binaries in dist/ (needs cargo-zigbuild on macOS)

Release builds stamp the version, commit, channel, and the release public key through environment variables (SERVEROS_VERSION, SERVEROS_COMMIT, SERVEROS_CHANNEL, SERVEROS_RELEASE_PUBKEY). A binary built without a public key cannot install updates, which is the safe failure.

Gateway

serveros-gateway (crates/serveros-gateway) is the panel-side end of the control channel. It terminates each daemon's mutual-TLS WebSocket, reads the certificate serial, asks the panel (POST /api/gateway/hello) which machine that is, and then relays: daemon envelopes are batched to /api/gateway/machines/{uid}/ingest, and the panel pushes commands through the gateway's loopback API (POST /machines/{uid}/commands). Browser terminals and log tails attach to /streams/{session} with a ticket the panel signed, so PTY bytes never pass through PHP.

php artisan daemon:ca init                      # once, in the panel
php artisan daemon:ca issue-server --host gateway.example.com --out /etc/serveros/gateway
make gateway && cp target/release/serveros-gateway /usr/local/bin/
cp deploy/gateway.env.example /etc/serveros/gateway.env   # fill in GATEWAY_SECRET
cp deploy/serveros-gateway.service /etc/systemd/system/ && systemctl enable --now serveros-gateway

It keeps no state: restart it and daemons reconnect with backoff.

Integrations

The daemon drives host tools it does not replace. The defaults are what the installer would pick on a fresh Ubuntu box; an existing server keeps what it has by changing [integrations] in /etc/serveros/daemon.toml:

[integrations]
proxy = "caddy"      # caddy | nginx | none
firewall = "ufw"     # ufw | nftables | iptables | none
Proxy: one site file per deployed service in a directory ServerOS owns (/etc/caddy/serveros.d or /etc/nginx/serveros.d), validated before reload, reverted if validation fails. Caddy handles TLS itself; with nginx, TLS stays whatever certbot or the operator set up.
Wildcard subdomains: a service on *.example.com gets a Caddy site with on-demand TLS, so each subdomain gets its own certificate the first time it's visited, over the usual HTTP challenge, with no DNS provider. The daemon adds on_demand_tls { ask … } to the Caddyfile's global options and answers Caddy's question on 127.0.0.1:47019, saying yes only for a name one label under a wildcard in its own site files. A Caddyfile that already sets on_demand_tls is left alone.
Cloudflare Tunnel: the tunnel job (action: up with the tunnel's token, or down) runs cloudflared as the serveros-tunnel systemd unit, installed from Cloudflare's package repository (apt, dnf or yum) if it's missing. The token is kept root-only in /etc/serveros/tunnel.env and read by the unit, so it's never on a command line, in a log or in the job ledger. While the tunnel is up, Caddy serves every app domain over plain HTTP on port 80 (the tunnel's edge does HTTPS; apps get X-Forwarded-Proto: https), marked by .plain-http in serveros.d; down puts HTTPS back. A failed up leaves the machine as it was. Point the tunnel's routes (published applications, *.example.com say) at http://localhost:80. Visitors' addresses arrive in Cloudflare's CF-Connecting-IP header. Gated as tunnel.write and refused in read-only mode.
Firewall: ufw rules pass through verbatim. nftables and iptables take the port form (22/tcp, from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 5432); nftables rules live in a table ServerOS owns (inet serveros).
Project networks: the network job gives a project its own WireGuard network across machines. Each machine gets an interface named sos{network} (sosp7k2q9; network ids are at most 12 characters, so the name fits the kernel's 15), one address on it, and exactly the peers the panel lists. Services are offered on that address by small TCP forwarders that only point at loopback or the Docker bridge. The firewall lets in the UDP port, the network on its interface, and local containers reaching an offered port, only over Docker's bridges (docker*, br-*: a provider network in 172.16.0.0/12 isn't let in); nftables and iptables keep these in a chain of the network's own (net_{id}, SOS-{id}). With nftables they also go, tagged serveros:net_{id}, at the top of every other inet table's input chain, since a policy drop there would otherwise win. The private key is made on the machine, kept root-only in /var/lib/serveros/networks, and never sent; networks come back up when the daemon starts. wireguard-tools is installed if wg is missing. The job's fields, checks and results, and how the panel copies a database between machines over the network, are in docs/project-networks.md.
Links: the default panel (SERVEROS_PANEL_URL) and the docs base (SERVEROS_DOCS_URL) are build-time environment variables, and the release download allowlist is [updates] allowed_hosts.
Error reports

When the daemon crashes or logs an error, it sends a short report to ServerOS (we use Sentry) so we can find and fix the bug. Reports are scrubbed on the machine before they go: no hostname, IP addresses, users or request data, and anything that looks like a token, key, password or env value is replaced with [redacted]. No file contents are ever attached. Each report carries the daemon's version and the machine id the panel gave it at enrolment, nothing else that identifies the box.

Only our release builds report; a build from source sends nothing unless you give it an address. To turn reports off, either:

[error_reports]
enabled = false

in /etc/serveros/daemon.toml, or SERVEROS_ERROR_REPORTS=0 in the service's environment (systemctl edit serverosd). You can also switch them on or off for a machine from its machine policy in the panel. That writes the same enabled setting and takes effect straight away, no restart. SERVEROS_ERROR_REPORTS=0 always wins: with it set, the reporting code is never started and the panel can't turn it back on. To send reports to your own Sentry instead, set dsn = "https://..." in the same section, or SERVEROS_SENTRY_DSN. serverosd debug sentry-test sends one test report and tells you whether it arrived. The gateway follows the same two environment variables.

Fixtures

make messy-check builds the daemon for Linux in Docker and runs its discovery scan against tests/fixtures/messy-server: nginx in front of a pm2 app, postgres and redis started by hand, a game server in screen, a nohup'd script, a cron job, and a letsencrypt-style certificate. The checks assert each is found, classified, and attributed to the right manager. Two things still need a real VM rather than a container: systemd unit discovery (containers have no systemd, so only the honest "not reachable" path runs) and the Docker socket.

Updates

Automatic updates follow daemon.toml: they can be turned off, pinned to a version, restricted to a channel, or limited to a maintenance window. A major version change always waits for a person to approve it. Releases carry min_from, so a daemon too far behind is told to step through an intermediate release. The old binary stays beside the new one, and a new binary that fails to reconnect three times is rolled back automatically.

Protocol

Every message is an envelope with a protocol major, a monotonic sequence number, an id, and a typed payload. Changes within a major are additive; a breaking change is a new driver in daemon-protocol, and the old driver keeps shipping until no supported daemon speaks i

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Install ServerOS on your own server, with Docker:
#
#   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/serveroshq/panel/main/docker/self-hosted/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- --domain=panel.example.com --email=you@example.com
#
# or from a checkout: sudo bash docker/self-hosted/install.sh --domain=... --email=...
#
# It runs the official image, ghcr.io/serveroshq/panel: the open source
# panel (AGPL-3.0) plus the paid features, in the commercial panel-ee
# package under its own license. Without a license key it works exactly
# like the community edition; add a key in Settings › License to turn the
# paid features on. --image runs another, like a community edition you
# built from source (docs/self-hosting.md, "Editions").
#
# The panel answers on the domain and each workspace on a subdomain of it,
# so before you start point both at this server: an A (or AAAA) record for
# panel.example.com and one for *.panel.example.com. Ports 80 and 443 (the
# panel, with free Let's Encrypt certificates) and 8443 (where your
# machines connect) must be open.
#
# Behind a Cloudflare Tunnel instead (--tunnel-token), ports 80 and 443
# stay closed: cloudflared carries the panel's traffic and Cloudflare does
# HTTPS. Machines still connect to the gateway directly, on a name of its
# own that points at this server, DNS only (--gateway-host), port 8443.
#
# Options:
#   --domain=NAME      the panel's address (required)
#   --email=ADDRESS    for Let's Encrypt's expiry notices (required, unless
#                      behind a tunnel)
#   --tunnel-token=TOKEN
#                      run behind this Cloudflare Tunnel (the token from the
#                      tunnel's install command in Cloudflare, Networking > Tunnels)
#   --gateway-host=NAME
#                      where machines connect, behind a tunnel (like
#                      gateway.example.com, DNS only, pointing here)
#   --dir=PATH         where it lives (default /opt/serveros)
#   --version=X.Y.Z    an image version instead of the latest
#   --image=NAME       another image (default ghcr.io/serveroshq/panel,
#                      the official one); switches an install to it
#
# Running it again keeps your settings and data, and brings the install up
# to date. Afterwards, serveros-panel does upgrades and backups.
set -euo pipefail

DOMAIN="${SERVEROS_DOMAIN:-}"
EMAIL="${ACME_EMAIL:-}"
DIR="${SERVEROS_DIR:-/opt/serveros}"
IMAGE_NAME="ghcr.io/serveroshq/panel"
VERSION="latest"
IMAGE_GIVEN=0
TUNNEL_TOKEN="${CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN:-}"
GATEWAY_HOST="${SERVEROS_GATEWAY_HOST:-}"

say() { printf '\033[1m==>\033[0m %s\n' "$*"; }
warn() { printf '\033[33mwarning:\033[0m %s\n' "$*" >&2; }
fail() { printf '\033[31merror:\033[0m %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }

for arg in "$@"; do
    case "$arg" in
        --domain=*) DOMAIN="${arg#--domain=}" ;;
        --email=*) EMAIL="${arg#--email=}" ;;
        --dir=*) DIR="${arg#--dir=}" ;;
        --version=*) VERSION="${arg#--version=}"; VERSION="${VERSION#v}" ;;
        --image=*) IMAGE_NAME="${arg#--image=}"; IMAGE_GIVEN=1 ;;
        --tunnel-token=*) TUNNEL_TOKEN="${arg#--tunnel-token=}" ;;
        --gateway-host=*) GATEWAY_HOST="${arg#--gateway-host=}" ;;
        -h|--help) sed -n '2,45p' "$0" 2>/dev/null | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'; exit 0 ;;
        *) fail "unknown option $arg (see --help)" ;;
    esac
done
IMAGE="${IMAGE_NAME}:${VERSION}"

[ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ] || fail "run it as root (with sudo)."
[ "$(uname -s)" = "Linux" ] || fail "ServerOS self-hosting runs on Linux."

ask() {
    # ask VAR "Question": from the terminal, even when piped from curl.
    local answer=""
    if [ -r /dev/tty ]; then
        read -r -p "$2 " answer < /dev/tty || true
    fi
    printf -v "$1" '%s' "$answer"
}

# An existing install keeps its settings.
if [ -f "$DIR/.env" ]; then
    existing() { grep -E "^$1=" "$DIR/.env" | tail -n1 | cut -d= -f2- || true; }
    DOMAIN="${DOMAIN:-$(existing SERVEROS_DOMAIN)}"
    EMAIL="${EMAIL:-$(existing ACME_EMAIL)}"
    TUNNEL_TOKEN="${TUNNEL_TOKEN:-$(existing CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN)}"
    GATEWAY_HOST="${GATEWAY_HOST:-$(existing SERVEROS_GATEWAY_HOST)}"
fi
# The whole install command pasted: the token is its last word.
TUNNEL_TOKEN="$(printf '%s' "$TUNNEL_TOKEN" | awk '{print $NF}')"
TUNNEL=0
[ -z "$TUNNEL_TOKEN" ] || TUNNEL=1

is_domain() { printf '%s' "$1" | grep -Eq '^[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9-]*[a-z0-9])?(\.[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9-]*[a-z0-9])?)+$'; }
bare() { printf '%s' "$1" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed -e 's|^https\?://||' -e 's|/.*$||' -e 's|:[0-9]*$||'; }

[ -n "$DOMAIN" ] || ask DOMAIN "The panel's domain (like panel.example.com):"
DOMAIN="$(bare "$DOMAIN")"
is_domain "$DOMAIN" || fail "\"$DOMAIN\" isn't a domain name. Use --domain=panel.example.com"
if [ "$TUNNEL" = 1 ]; then
    printf '%s' "$TUNNEL_TOKEN" | grep -Eq '^[A-Za-z0-9+/=_-]{40,4096}$' \
        || fail "that isn't a Cloudflare Tunnel token. Copy it from the tunnel's install command in Cloudflare (Networking > Tunnels)."
    [ -n "$GATEWAY_HOST" ] || ask GATEWAY_HOST "Where machines connect, a name pointing straight at this server, DNS only (like gateway.example.com):"
    GATEWAY_HOST="$(bare "$GATEWAY_HOST")"
    is_domain "$GATEWAY_HOST" || fail "give the gateway a name with --gateway-host=gateway.example.com"
    [ "$GATEWAY_HOST" != "$DOMAIN" ] || fail "machines can't connect through the tunnel, so the gateway needs a name of its own, not $DOMAIN (like gateway.example.com)."
else
    [ -n "$EMAIL" ] || ask EMAIL "Your email, for Let's Encrypt:"
    printf '%s' "$EMAIL" | grep -q '@' || fail "give an email address with --email=you@example.com"
fi

# Docker, with Compose.
if ! command -v docker >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    say "Installing Docker"
    curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
fi
docker compose version >/dev/null 2>&1 || fail "Docker Compose v2 isn't installed (the docker-compose-plugin package)."
systemctl enable --now docker >/dev/null 2>&1 || true

# Ports another program already holds.
if command -v ss >/dev/null 2>&1 && [ ! -f "$DIR/compose.yaml" ]; then
    # Behind a tunnel the panel only listens on this server, on 18080 and 18443.
    ports="80 443 8443"
    [ "$TUNNEL" = 0 ] || ports="18080 18443 8443"
    for port in $ports; do
        if ss -ltnH "sport = :$port" | grep -q .; then
            fail "port $port is already in use ($(ss -ltnpH "sport = :$port" | sed -n 's/.*users:((\"\([^\"]*\)\".*/\1/p' | head -n1)). ServerOS needs $(printf '%s' "$ports" | sed 's/ /, /g')."
        fi
    done
fi

# DNS: a warning only, since it may still be on its way.
public_ip="$(curl -fsS4 --max-time 5 https://api.ipify.org 2>/dev/null || true)"
check_dns() {
    local name="$1" found
    found="$(getent ahostsv4 "$name" 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR==1 {print $1}')"
    if [ -z "$found" ]; then
        warn "$name doesn't resolve yet. Add an A record pointing at ${public_ip:-this server}."
    elif [ -n "$public_ip" ] && [ "$found" != "$public_ip" ]; then
        warn "$name points at $found, not this server ($public_ip)."
    fi
}
if [ "$TUNNEL" = 1 ]; then
    # The panel's names come from the tunnel's routes (set up
    # below); the gateway's must point here without Cloudflare's proxy.
    check_dns "$GATEWAY_HOST"
else
    check_dns "$DOMAIN"
    check_dns "serveros-check-$RANDOM.$DOMAIN"
fi

mkdir -p "$DIR"
chmod 700 "$DIR"
cd "$DIR"

random() { head -c "$1" /dev/urandom | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n'; }

if [ ! -f .env ]; then
    say "Writing $DIR/.env"
    umask 077
    cat > .env <<EOF
# ServerOS, self-hosted. Change a setting, then: docker compose up -d
SERVEROS_DOMAIN=$DOMAIN
ACME_EMAIL=$EMAIL
SERVEROS_IMAGE=$IMAGE

# Generated for this install. Keep a copy somewhere safe: backups need
# APP_KEY to be read back.
APP_KEY=base64:$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)
DB_PASSWORD=$(random 24)
DAEMON_GATEWAY_SECRET=$(random 32)

# The key ServerOS signs daemon releases with. Machines check the daemon
# they download against it before installing it.
DAEMON_RELEASE_PUBKEY=5245716675785d7bf5dc36d783fa5c690c705da4d542082f398e3e79543d06f8

# Email, for invitations, alerts and password resets: set it up in the
# web installer, or here. Until it's set up, emails are only written to
# the log (docker compose logs queue).
# MAIL_MAILER=smtp
# MAIL_HOST=smtp.example.com
# MAIL_PORT=587
# MAIL_USERNAME=
# MAIL_PASSWORD=
# MAIL_FROM_ADDRESS=serveros@example.com
# MAIL_FROM_NAME=ServerOS

# Once a day the panel sends serveros.com an anonymous ping: a random id for
# this install, its version, whether it's licensed and how many workspaces,
# people and machines it has. Nothing that says who or where you are.
# See exactly what it sends: serveros-panel artisan install:ping --show
# Turn it off:
# SERVEROS_TELEMETRY=false
EOF
    umask 022
elif [ "$VERSION" != "latest" ] || [ "$IMAGE_GIVEN" = 1 ] || ! grep -q '^SERVEROS_IMAGE=' .env; then
    if grep -q '^SERVEROS_IMAGE=' .env; then
        sed -i "s|^SERVEROS_IMAGE=.*|SERVEROS_IMAGE=$IMAGE|" .env
    else
        printf 'SERVEROS_IMAGE=%s\n' "$IMAGE" >> .env
    fi
fi
IMAGE="$(grep -E '^SERVEROS_IMAGE=' .env | tail -n1 | cut -d= -f2-)"

# set_env KEY VALUE: replaces the setting, or adds it.
set_env() {
    local rest
    rest="$(grep -vE "^$1=" .env || true)"
    umask 077
    printf '%s\n%s=%s\n' "$rest" "$1" "$2" > .env.new && mv .env.new .env
    umask 022
}
if [ "$TUNNEL" = 1 ]; then
    # cloudflared (COMPOSE_PROFILES=tunnel) carries the panel's traffic, so the
    # panel only listens on this server. The gateway reaches the panel inside
    # Docker with Caddy's own certificate (local_certs), since Let's Encrypt
    # can't reach it here.
    set_env SERVEROS_TUNNEL cloudflare
    set_env CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN "$TUNNEL_TOKEN"
    set_env SERVEROS_GATEWAY_HOST "$GATEWAY_HOST"
    set_env COMPOSE_PROFILES tunnel
    set_env HTTP_PORT 127.0.0.1:18080
    set_env HTTPS_PORT 127.0.0.1:18443
    set_env CADDY_GLOBAL_OPTIONS local_certs
    set_env GATEWAY_PANEL_CA /gateway/panel-ca.crt
fi
grep -q '^DAEMON_RELEASE_PUBKEY=' .env || printf 'DAEMON_RELEASE_PUBKEY=%s\n' "5245716675785d7bf5dc36d783fa5c690c705da4d542082f398e3e79543d06f8" >> .env

say "Pulling $IMAGE"
if ! docker pull "$IMAGE"; then
    # An image built on this server (docker build) has nowhere to come from.
    docker image inspect "$IMAGE" >/dev/null 2>&1 || fail "couldn't pull $IMAGE, and there's no image by that name here."
    warn "couldn't pull $IMAGE: using the one already here."
fi
# The compose file and the serveros-panel command come from the image, so
# they always match the version that runs.
image_compose="$(docker run --rm --entrypoint cat "$IMAGE" /app/docker/self-hosted/compose.yaml)"
# An image from before tunnels (1.1.0 and older) has no cloudflared and can't
# serve the panel to one, so it would only fail to start.
if [ "$TUNNEL" = 1 ] && ! printf '%s' "$image_compose" | grep -q cloudflared; then
    fail "$IMAGE doesn't support Cloudflare Tunnels (1.2.0 and later do). Run the script again with --version=1.2.0, or a newer one."
fi
printf '%s\n' "$image_compose" > compose.yaml
docker run --rm --entrypoint cat "$IMAGE" /app/docker/self-hosted/serveros-panel > /usr/local/bin/serveros-panel
chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/serveros-panel
# Only a compose file that gives Redis the password can have one.
if grep -q requirepass compose.yaml && ! grep -q '^REDIS_PASSWORD=.' .env; then
    sed -i '/^REDIS_PASSWORD=/d' .env
    printf 'REDIS_PASSWORD=%s\n' "$(random 24)" >> .env
fi

say "Starting ServerOS"
docker compose up -d --remove-orphans

tries=0
until docker compose exec -T web curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8081/up >/dev/null 2>&1; do
    tries=$((tries + 1))
    [ "$tries" -lt 150 ] || fail "the panel didn't start in 5 minutes. See what happened: serveros-panel logs web"
    sleep 2
done
docker compose exec -T web php artisan daemon:sync-releases --no-interaction >/dev/null 2>&1 \
    || warn "couldn't fetch the daemon releases from serveros.com yet. The panel tries again every hour; until then,
